formation.title: The Rise of Persia
formation.text:
The Iranian Plateau stands united under a single crown. From the Zagros Mountains to the shores of the Caspian, from the deserts of Khorasan to the marshes of Mesopotamia, the diverse peoples of Persia answer to one sovereign. This is the moment that Cyrus and Darius once knew, the birth of an empire that stretches across continents and cultures.

But the character of this empire remains to be decided. Shall we ride forth as conquerors, as the Achaemenids and Sassanids before us? Shall we build Isfahan into the wonder of the world, a capital that makes the courts of Europe weep with envy? Or shall we forge the religious unity that will define Persia for centuries, becoming the unshakeable bastion of the Shia faith?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: We shall ride as King of Kings!

modifiers.name: Shahanshah: King of Kings
modifiers.text: The throne of Persia demands dominion. As Shahanshah, the King of Kings, our armies shall thunder across the Iranian Plateau and beyond, carrying the banner of empire to every corner of the known world. The cavalry that crushed the Ottomans at Chaldiran and the Uzbeks at Merv rides again.

options.text: Isfahan shall be half the world.

modifiers.name: Isfahan Nesf-e Jahan
modifiers.text: Isfahan is half the world, so the proverb declares. Under the Shahs, Persia shall become a beacon of civilization where art, commerce, and learning flourish. The grand bazaars will hum with trade from China to Europe, and the beauty of Persian architecture will inspire awe across the ages.

options.text: We are the guardians of the true faith.

modifiers.name: Guardian of the Shia Faith
modifiers.text: Persia stands as the fortress of Twelver Shiism against a world of Sunni empires. Through the authority of the Shah and the wisdom of the ulama, the nation will forge an unbreakable bond between state and faith. Religious unity will be the foundation upon which an enduring empire is built.

advances.name: Ribat Tradition
advances.text: The ribat network, fortified way-stations along Persia's trade routes, served as both military garrisons and shelters for travelers, projecting Persian power across the vast interior.

advances.name: Qanat Irrigation
advances.text: The qanat, underground aqueducts that carry water from mountain aquifers to arid lowlands, is one of Persia's greatest engineering achievements, enabling agriculture in otherwise uninhabitable regions.

advances.name: Bazaar Economy
advances.text: The covered bazaar, or bazar-e bozorg, is the economic heart of every Persian city, a vast labyrinth of vaulted passages where guilds organize production, merchants negotiate prices, and the wazarbed oversees commercial order.

advances.name: Persian Diplomatic Tradition
advances.text: The Persian court has maintained sophisticated diplomatic traditions since Achaemenid times, employing elaborate protocol, multilingual envoys, and the strategic art of gift-giving to manage relations with neighboring empires.

advances.name: Keshikchi Guard
advances.text: The Keshikchi, royal bodyguard cavalry inherited from the Timurid and Mongol traditions, form an elite guard of horsemen sworn to protect the person of the sovereign. Selected from the finest warriors of noble families, they serve as both shock cavalry and a symbol of royal authority.

advances.name: Caspian Silk Industry
advances.text: The lush provinces of Gilan and Mazandaran along the Caspian coast produce some of the finest raw silk in the world. Shah Abbas centralized this industry into a royal monopoly, making silk Persia's most valuable export to European markets.

advances.name: Persian Miniature Painting
advances.text: The Persian miniature tradition, perfected by masters like Bihzad, combines exquisite detail with vibrant color to illustrate the great works of Persian literature. Court workshops in Tabriz, Qazvin, and Isfahan produce illuminated manuscripts that are treasured from Constantinople to Delhi.

advances.name: Royal Court Culture
advances.text: The Persian royal court has long been a center of cosmopolitan culture, where poets, musicians, painters, and scholars from across the Islamic world gather under the Shah's patronage. This tradition of cultural openness allows Persia to absorb and synthesize diverse influences.

advances.name: Caravanserai Network
advances.text: Shah Abbas commissioned the construction of caravanserais at regular intervals along all major trade routes, fortified inns offering free lodging, stabling, and security to merchants. This massive infrastructure program transformed Persia into the most welcoming land for overland trade in the entire Middle East.

advances.name: Chapar Riders
advances.text: The chapar system, a network of mounted couriers maintaining relay stations across the empire, traces its origins to the Achaemenid Empire's famous 'Royal Road' postal service. These swift riders carry dispatches, intelligence, and royal commands across vast distances at remarkable speed.

advances.name: Royal Workshops
advances.text:
The karkhane, royal workshops attached to the court, produce luxury goods of extraordinary quality. Under Safavid patronage, these workshops in Isfahan employ hundreds of craftsmen working in silk weaving, carpet knotting, metalwork, and ceramics, their products destined for both domestic consumption and export.

Available in: Karkhane

advances.name: Haft Rang Tilework
advances.text:
The haft rang (seven-color) tile technique allows Persian artisans to create the stunning polychromatic facades that adorn mosques, palaces, and madrasas across Iran. The intricate geometric and floral patterns of Persian tilework represent one of the highest achievements of Islamic decorative art.

Available in: Karkhane

advances.name: Divan Governance
advances.text: The Persian divan, the royal council of ministers, is the administrative backbone of the empire. The grand vizier, provincial governors, and specialized officials manage taxation, justice, and correspondence through an elaborate bureaucratic tradition refined over centuries.

advances.name: Termeh Looms of Kerman and Yazd
advances.text:
Under the Safavids the weavers of Kerman and Yazd turned the soft down of the Kerman goat into termeh, a close patterned cloth of many colours. It was worn at court as sashes and coats, given by the Shah as robes of honour, and carried abroad by the merchants of the Gulf ports.

Available in: Karkhane

advances.name: Zamburak Corps
advances.text: The zamburak, a swivel gun mounted on camelback, gives Persian armies mobile artillery suited to the deserts and plains of the Iranian Plateau. First employed at scale by Nader Shah, the zamburakchi corps proved devastatingly effective at the Battle of Karnal.

event.title: The Zamburak Corps
event.text:
A new innovation has appeared on the battlefield, the zamburak, a small swivel cannon mounted on the back of a camel. These mobile artillery pieces combine the speed of cavalry with the firepower of cannon, allowing Persian forces to bring devastating firepower to bear in the open deserts and plains where conventional artillery would bog down.

The zamburakchi corps proved decisive at the Battle of Karnal in 1739, where Nader Shah's camel-mounted guns shattered the Mughal army and its war elephants. The corps operates in batteries of dozens or even hundreds of camels, creating a mobile wall of fire that can redeploy faster than any wheeled artillery. This Persian innovation will give our armies a unique tactical advantage across the arid landscapes of our domain.

options.text: The camels of war shall thunder across our enemies.

advances.name: Theological Colleges
advances.text: The Safavid state invested heavily in madrasas dedicated to Twelver Shia theology, importing scholars from Lebanon, Bahrain, and Iraq to establish a new religious intelligentsia. These institutions became the intellectual foundation of Shia Islam in Persia.

advances.name: Isfahan Nesf-e Jahan
advances.text: Isfahan nesf-e jahan, Isfahan is half the world. Under Shah Abbas, the capital was transformed with the magnificent Naqsh-e Jahan Square, the Shah Mosque, the Ali Qapu Palace, and the Chahar Bagh Avenue, creating one of the most beautiful cities on earth.

event.title: Isfahan: Half the World
event.text:
Shah Abbas has chosen Isfahan as his capital, and the city has been transformed beyond recognition. The magnificent Naqsh-e Jahan Square, one of the largest public squares in the world, stands as the beating heart of the empire. The Shah Mosque's turquoise dome gleams in the sun, the Ali Qapu Palace overlooks all commerce, and the Bazaar-e Bozorg stretches for kilometers through vaulted corridors.

Foreigners who visit declare that Isfahan is indeed 'half the world,' for here one may find everything that exists elsewhere. The Chahar Bagh Avenue, lined with gardens and pavilions, connects the Armenian quarter of New Julfa to the royal palaces. Shall we invest in Isfahan's cultural magnificence, making it a monument to Persian civilization? Or shall we channel its energy into commercial networks that will enrich the entire empire?

options.text: Let Isfahan's beauty inspire the ages.

modifiers.name: Glory of Isfahan
modifiers.text: Isfahan's architectural splendor and cultural patronage have made it a wonder of the world.

options.text: Let Isfahan's bazaars enrich the empire.

modifiers.name: Commerce of Isfahan
modifiers.text: Isfahan's bazaars and trade networks have made it the commercial heart of the Middle East.

advances.name: Tuyul Land Grant System
advances.text: The tuyul system assigns crown land revenues to military commanders and officials in lieu of salary. This arrangement ensures the loyalty of the provincial elite while allowing the central government to extract revenue without a large civilian bureaucracy.

advances.name: Shia Conversion Policy
advances.text: The Safavid transformation of Persia from a predominantly Sunni land to the heartland of Twelver Shiism is one of the most dramatic religious changes in Islamic history. State-sponsored conversion, the importation of Shia scholars, and the establishment of religious institutions created an enduring national identity.

event.title: The Conversion of Persia
event.text:
The transformation of Persia from a predominantly Sunni land to the heartland of Twelver Shiism is one of the most dramatic religious upheavals in Islamic history. Under Shah Ismail, the process began with the declaration that Shia Islam was the state religion. Sunni ulama were given the choice of conversion, exile, or death. Arab Shia scholars were brought from Jabal Amil in Lebanon, from Bahrain, and from southern Iraq to fill the theological void and establish new institutions of learning.

The Safavid state now faces a choice in how to consolidate this transformation. Shall we pursue zealous enforcement of doctrinal purity, using the power of the state to ensure complete religious conformity? Or shall we invest in theological scholarship, building the intellectual foundations that will make Twelver Shiism self-sustaining through the strength of its learning?

options.text: Enforce the purity of the faith.

modifiers.name: Shia Zealotry
modifiers.text: The enforced purity of Twelver Shiism has created deep religious unity across Persian lands.

options.text: Invest in Shia scholarship and learning.

modifiers.name: Shia Scholarship
modifiers.text: Investment in theological colleges and scholarly tradition has made Persia the intellectual center of the Shia world.

advances.name: Shahsavan Tribal Confederation
advances.text: The Shahsavan, literally 'those who love the Shah', are a tribal confederation organized by Shah Abbas to counterbalance the power of the Qizilbash aristocracy. Loyal directly to the throne, they provide reliable cavalry that serves as a check on overmighty tribal chieftains.

advances.name: Imperial Postal System
advances.text: The chapar-khaneh postal relay system maintains a network of stations across the empire, each equipped with fresh horses and riders. This system, descended from the Achaemenid angareion, allows royal commands and intelligence to travel from one end of Persia to the other in a matter of days.

advances.name: Persian Gulf Fleet
advances.text: The Afsharid naval program, initiated by Nader Shah, established a Persian fleet based at Bushire on the Persian Gulf. Though Persia has traditionally been a land power, the gulf fleet projects power along vital maritime trade routes and challenges the dominance of European naval squadrons.

advances.name: Nastaliq Calligraphy
advances.text: The nastaliq script, developed in Persia as an elegant cursive style, became the defining calligraphic tradition of the Persian-speaking world. Its flowing curves and graceful proportions adorn manuscripts, inscriptions, and administrative documents, embodying the Persian aesthetic ideal.

advances.name: Maragheh Observatory Tradition
advances.text: The Maragheh Observatory, founded under the Ilkhanids by Nasir al-Din Tusi, established a scientific tradition in Persia that persisted for centuries. Persian astronomers and mathematicians continued to make contributions to observational astronomy, optics, and algebra long after the observatory itself fell into ruin.

advances.name: Nizam-i Jadid Reform
advances.text: Influenced by the military successes of European powers, Persian reformers advocate for a 'New Order', reorganizing the army along European lines with professional officers, regular drill, standardized equipment, and modern tactics.

event.title: The New Order: Military Reform
event.text:
Persian observers returning from Europe bring troubling reports. The armies of France, Prussia, and Russia have undergone transformations that make them far more effective than the traditional forces of the East. Regular drill, standardized equipment, professional officer corps, and systematic logistics have created military machines of unprecedented efficiency.

The question facing the Persian court is how to respond. Some argue that Persia must adopt European methods wholesale, importing instructors, purchasing modern weapons, and reorganizing the army along European lines. Others insist that Persian military traditions have their own strengths (cavalry mobility, knowledge of terrain, and the warrior spirit of the tribal levies) and that reform should synthesize the best of both worlds rather than abandoning centuries of Persian martial heritage.

options.text: Adopt European methods and discipline.

modifiers.name: European Military Drill
modifiers.text: Persian regiments now train according to European methods, with disciplined formations and modern tactics.

options.text: Synthesize the best of East and West.

modifiers.name: Persian Military Synthesis
modifiers.text: The best of Persian cavalry tradition has been combined with selective modern innovations.

advances.name: Qajar Modernization
advances.text: The Dar ul-Funun polytechnic, founded in Tehran in 1851, was the first modern institution of higher learning in Persia. It taught European languages, medicine, engineering, and military science, training a new generation of Persian professionals who would drive the country's modernization.

advances.name: Constitutional Movement
advances.text: The Persian Constitutional Revolution represents the aspiration for modern governance, a written constitution, an elected parliament (the Majlis), and the rule of law. This movement drew support from intellectuals, merchants, and progressive clergy who sought to limit royal absolutism.

event.title: The Constitutional Awakening
event.text:
A remarkable movement has emerged among Persian intellectuals, merchants, and progressive clergy. Inspired by constitutional developments in Europe and the Ottoman Tanzimat reforms, they argue that Persia needs a fundamental transformation of its system of government. The absolute power of the Shah, they contend, has led to corruption, stagnation, and foreign exploitation.

The Constitutional Revolution represents a watershed moment in Persian history, the first modern attempt to limit royal authority through a written constitution and an elected parliament, the Majlis. Whether it succeeds fully or is partially reversed, it marks the beginning of Persia's engagement with modern political thought and the aspiration for a government accountable to its people.

options.text: The voice of the people shall be heard.

advances.name: Persian Trade Reform
advances.text: The modernization of Persian commerce (including the establishment of customs houses, standardized weights and measures, and modern banking) opens the economy to international trade while protecting domestic producers from foreign exploitation.

destiny.name: Destiny of Persia
destiny.text: Persia has risen. The throne of the Shahs commands a vast domain from the Zagros to the Hindu Kush, and its many peoples answer to one crown. Now the character of this empire must be forged: through conquest or through civilization.

event.title: The Destiny of Persia
event.text:
The crown of Persia has been claimed, and the ancient lands of the Shahs are once more united under a single sovereign. From the snow-capped peaks of the Zagros to the sun-baked shores of the Persian Gulf, the diverse peoples of Iran answer to one throne.

But unification is merely the beginning. The great empires of Persia (the Achaemenids, the Sassanids, the Safavids) were not content merely to rule the plateau. Each sought to leave an indelible mark upon the world, whether through conquest, commerce, or culture.

What destiny awaits this new Persian empire?

options.text: Our destiny shall be written in the stars.

destiny.name: The Shahanshah Rides
destiny.text: Reclaim the lands of the ancient empires. Take Baghdad, seat of the Abbasid Caliphate, and Samarkand, jewel of Transoxiana. The King of Kings demands dominion over all the lands between the Tigris and the Oxus.

conditions.text: Own Baghdad, or a subject owns it
Own Samarkand, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Shahanshah Rides
event.text:
Baghdad has fallen to Persian arms, and the ancient cities of Transoxiana acknowledge the Shahanshah's sovereignty. From the banks of the Tigris to the orchards of Samarkand, the lands that once formed the heart of the Islamic world now bow to the Persian crown.

The conquest of Baghdad carries immense symbolic weight: the city of the Caliphs, the seat of the House of Wisdom, now flies the banner of Persia. And with Samarkand, the tomb of Timur himself is in Persian hands. The Shahanshah has announced to the world that the age of Persian empire has returned.

options.text: The King of Kings has spoken.

destiny.name: Master of Iran-Zamin
destiny.text: Extend Persian hegemony from Damascus in the west to the Caucasus in the north. The Shahanshah's writ must run through the Fertile Crescent and the lands of the Shirvanshah alike.

conditions.text: Own Damascus, or a subject owns it
Own Baku, or a subject owns it

event.title: Master of Iran-Zamin
event.text:
The boundaries of Persian power have expanded far beyond the Iranian Plateau. Damascus, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on earth, acknowledges Persian suzerainty. The oil fires of Baku on the Caspian shore illuminate a new frontier of Persian influence in the Caucasus.

The Shahanshah now commands a realm that recalls the extent of the Sassanid Empire at its greatest. The question before the court is how to press this advantage. Some generals urge an aggressive posture: the wrath of the Shahanshah must be felt by all who resist. Others counsel the restoration of the ancient satrapy system, binding conquered lands through administration rather than terror.

options.text: Let our enemies tremble before us.

modifiers.name: Wrath of the Shahanshah
modifiers.text: The Shahanshah's fury is legendary. Enemies who resist face brutal siege and total subjugation, driving the costs of defiance beyond what any foe can bear.

options.text: Restore the wisdom of the satraps.

modifiers.name: Restored Satrapy System
modifiers.text: The ancient Persian system of provincial governance through satrapies has been restored, allowing efficient annexation and integration of conquered territories.

destiny.name: Empire of Cyrus Reborn
destiny.text: Fulfill the ultimate Persian ambition: an empire stretching from Constantinople to Delhi, surpassing even the Achaemenids. Raise a great army to carry the war to both cities, and build up Mashhad, the capital of the conqueror of Delhi, with the spoils. Build the Apadana as a monument to this achievement: a throne room where envoys from every nation come to pay tribute.

conditions.text: Mashhad is ours and has been built up to a development of at least 22
Own Delhi, or a subject owns it
Own Constantinople, or a subject owns it

event.title: Empire of Cyrus Reborn
event.text:
It is done. Persian banners fly over Constantinople, that ancient jewel of empires, and over Delhi, gateway to the riches of India. The Shahanshah now rules a domain that surpasses even the dreams of Cyrus the Great: from the Bosphorus to the Ganges, from the Caucasus to the Persian Gulf.

This is not merely a military achievement but a civilizational statement. The construction of the Apadana (a grand audience hall modeled on the ancient Persepolis) will serve as the throne room of this reborn empire. Here, ambassadors from every nation will present themselves before the King of Kings.

But how shall this vast empire be governed? Through the iron discipline of an immortal military machine? Or through the art of diplomacy, binding diverse peoples in willing allegiance?

options.text: We are the Immortal Empire, eternal and unbreakable.

modifiers.name: The Immortal Empire
modifiers.text: Like the Ten Thousand Immortals of the Achaemenids, this empire endures through iron discipline and relentless expansion, its armies tireless and its intelligence networks far-reaching.

options.text: We are King of Nations, father to all peoples.

modifiers.name: King of Nations
modifiers.text: The Shahanshah rules not through fear alone but through the art of governance, binding diverse peoples in a web of diplomacy, offering peace to the willing and swift recovery to the devastated.

destiny.name: Silk Road Mastery
destiny.text: Establish Persia as the commercial nexus of the Silk Road. Ensure silk flows through the capital markets and fill the treasury with the wealth of east-west trade.

children.text: Silk is produced in the market
Silk is traded in the market

event.title: Silk Road Mastery
event.text:
The caravans that cross the Iranian Plateau carry the finest silk in the world: Persian silk, processed and finished by the artisans of Isfahan and Kerman. European merchants compete fiercely for access to Persian markets, while from the east, Chinese porcelain and Indian spices flow through the caravanserais that dot the Silk Road.

Persia sits at the crossroads of the world, and the Shahs have leveraged this position brilliantly. The royal silk monopoly channels vast wealth into the treasury, while the bazaars of the great cities hum with the commerce of nations. This is the foundation upon which a different kind of empire will be built: not one of conquest, but of commerce.

options.text: The wealth of the world flows through Persia.

destiny.name: Institutional Vanguard
destiny.text: Lead the Islamic world in institutional development. Build up Isfahan and raise there the Bazaar-e Bozorg, where the money changers of the Qaysariyya keep the accounts of the realm, and make the city a beacon of Persian civilization.

conditions.text: Isfahan is ours and has been built up to a development of at least 24
Isfahan is ours and a Bazaar-e Bozorg stands there

event.title: Institutional Vanguard
event.text:
Persia has built the institutions of a great state not as a follower but as a leader. The money changers of the Bazaar-e Bozorg in Isfahan rival the banking houses of Venice and Amsterdam, while Persian scholars and administrators have adapted new ideas to serve the needs of an ancient civilization.

This institutional sophistication gives Persia a profound advantage over its neighbors. The question is how to deploy it. Shah Abbas famously maintained royal monopolies over key industries, channeling their profits directly to the crown. But others argue that freeing the bazaars from royal control would unleash even greater commercial energy, turning every merchant into an engine of Persian prosperity.

options.text: The crown shall hold the monopolies.

modifiers.name: Royal Monopolies
modifiers.text: The Shah maintains monopolies over key industries, channeling commercial profits directly to the crown and funding a mercantilist state, though military readiness suffers from the focus on commerce.

options.text: Free the bazaars to trade without limit.

modifiers.name: Free Bazaars
modifiers.text: The bazaars of Persia trade freely without royal interference, attracting merchants from across the world and fostering diplomatic connections through open commerce.

destiny.name: Isfahan Nesf-e Jahan
destiny.text: Isfahan is half the world. Take Gamrun, the port Shah Abbas named Bandar Abbas, to carry its silk to the world, attract gems to the capital markets, and build the magnificent Naqsh-e Jahan Square, a monument proclaiming Persian splendor to every corner of the earth.

conditions.text: Own Gamrūn, or a subject owns it

children.text: Gems is produced in the market
Gems is traded in the market

event.title: Isfahan Nesf-e Jahan
event.text:
Isfahan is half the world. The old Persian proverb has become literal truth. The Naqsh-e Jahan Square (the Image of the World) stands complete, one of the largest and most beautiful public spaces ever constructed. The Shah Mosque's turquoise dome catches the light of dawn. The Ali Qapu Palace surveys the commercial bustle below. The Bazaar-e Bozorg stretches for kilometers through vaulted corridors where merchants from fifty nations trade in goods from every corner of the earth.

Foreigners who visit are struck speechless. This is not merely a city but a monument to what Persian civilization can achieve through commerce and culture rather than conquest. Shall Isfahan become a wonder that inspires ages to come? Or shall it serve as the hub of a global trading network that makes Persia the indispensable crossroads of the world?

options.text: Let Isfahan's wonder inspire eternity.

modifiers.name: Wonder of the World
modifiers.text: Isfahan's architectural and cultural achievements have made it a wonder of the world, pushing Persia toward innovation and concentrating the finest talent in the capital.

options.text: Let Isfahan be the crossroads of all trade.

modifiers.name: Crossroads of Trade
modifiers.text: Persia's position at the intersection of maritime and overland trade routes has been fully realized, with the Persian Gulf fleet securing commerce and an outward-looking policy engaging the wider world.

units.name: Keshikchi Guard
units.text: Elite royal bodyguard cavalry descended from the Timurid keshik tradition, sworn to protect the person of the Shah.

units.name: Chapar Rider
units.text: Swift mounted couriers of the Persian postal system, trained as light cavalry raiders when called to war.

units.name: Zamburak
units.text: Camel-mounted swivel guns that bring mobile artillery to the deserts and plains of the Iranian Plateau.

units.name: Zamburak Levy
units.text: Tribal levies equipped with camel-mounted swivel guns, raised from the nomadic peoples of Persia's arid interior.

units.name: Shahsavan Cavalry
units.text: Tribal cavalry from the Shahsavan confederation, organized as a counterweight to Qizilbash power and loyal directly to the Shah.

units.name: Nizam-i Jadid Guard
units.text: Reformed Persian infantry trained in European drill and tactics, equipped with modern firearms and bayonets.

units.name: Persian Gulf Galley
units.text: Fast galleys of the Afsharid naval program, designed for the shallow waters and strong currents of the Persian Gulf.

buildings.name: Ribat
buildings.text: A fortified way-station along Persian trade routes, serving as both military garrison and shelter for caravans.

buildings.name: Bazaar-e Bozorg
buildings.text: The grand covered bazaar, a vast labyrinth of vaulted passages where guilds, merchants, and artisans conduct the commercial life of the city.

buildings.name: Talambar
buildings.text: The raised, thatched rearing shed of Gilan and Mazandaran, where silkworms are fed on mulberry leaves through the spring and their cocoons reeled into raw silk. Where the land bears silk, it yields more of it.

where.text: The location's raw material is Silk

buildings.name: Caravanserai
buildings.text: A fortified roadside inn offering free lodging and security to merchants, commissioned by the Shah to encourage trade across the empire.

buildings.name: Karkhane
buildings.text: A royal workshop producing luxury goods (silk textiles, fine carpets, and decorative ceramics) under the direct patronage of the Shah.

methods.name: Termeh Weaving
methods.unlocked_by: Termeh Looms of Kerman and Yazd

buildings.name: Madrasa-yi Sultani
buildings.text: A royal theological college training Shia scholars and jurists, strengthening the religious foundations of the Persian state.

buildings.name: Chapar-Khaneh
buildings.text: An imperial postal relay station equipped with fresh horses and riders, maintaining communications across the vast Persian Empire.

buildings.name: Dar ul-Funun
buildings.text: A modern polytechnic institute teaching European sciences, languages, and military arts, the vanguard of Persian modernization.

buildings.name: Apadana
buildings.text: A grand imperial audience hall inspired by the ancient Apadana at Persepolis, where ambassadors from every subject nation present tribute before the throne of the Shahanshah.

buildings.name: Naqsh-e Jahan Square
buildings.text: The Image of the World: a monumental public square and commercial center at the heart of Isfahan, combining the Shah Mosque, Ali Qapu Palace, and the entrance to the Grand Bazaar.

list.name: Divan-i-A'la
list.text: The supreme chancery of the realm, headed by the Vazir-i-Azam (Grand Vizier) under Shah Tahmasp and elaborated to its classical form by Shah Abbas I after his transfer of capital to Isfahan in 1598. The Divan-i-A'la presides over the diwans of finance, army, religious endowment, and the royal household, with the Grand Vizier hearing petitions each morning and signing edicts under the royal tughra. A capable vizier (Mirza Salman, Itimad al-Dawla) can make a young shah's reign; an empty vizierate leaves ministries feuding and revenue uncollected. The chancery exists to bind the diwans into a single throne, which is why the umara of the uymaqs hate it.

list.name: Sadr-us-Sudur
list.text: The chief sadr of the realm, supreme office of the Twelver Shia clergy, formalized by Shah Ismail I after his 1501 declaration of Twelver Shi'ism as state religion and split by Shah Tahmasp into the Sadr-i-Khassa (overseeing royal-domain endowments) and the Sadr-i-Mamalik (overseeing those of the realm at large). The sadr controls the waqf properties that finance the madrasas of Najaf, Karbala, and Isfahan, appoints Shaykhs al-Islam in the great cities, and supervises the long conversion of a population largely Sunni in 1501 into the Twelver heartland it has become by 1700. Under Shah Sultan Husayn the office gives way to the more militant Mulla-bashi, a clerical hardening that helps lose Isfahan to the Afghans in 1722.

list.name: Ghulam Household Corps
list.text: Shah Abbas I's standing army of the royal slaves, instituted around 1599 with the conversion and enrollment of Caucasian Christian boys (Georgians, Armenians, Circassians) captured or tributed from beyond the Caucasus, raised in the palace, and assigned offices and tuyul revenue grants as the shah's personal household. Modeled on the Ottoman devshirme and the Mamluk iqta, the ghulam corps gives the throne for the first time a body of officers and governors who owe nothing to the Turcoman uymaq chiefs and everything to the Padshah. By Shah Abbas's death in 1629 ghulams hold the great governorships of Fars, Azerbaijan, and Khorasan; the Qurchi-bashi is matched by a Qullar-aghasi who commands the slave corps in the field.

list.name: Qizilbash Uymaq Confederacy
list.text: The seven (later nine) Turcoman tribes (Shamlu, Ustajlu, Takkalu, Rumlu, Afshar, Qajar, Zulqadr, and others) whose cavalry put Shah Ismail on the throne at Sharur in 1501 and won the long campaigns against the Uzbeks of Bukhara and the Ottomans at Hoy. The Qizilbash, the 'red-heads' for their twelve-pleated taj of Shi'i devotion, provide the great offices of state (the Qurchi-bashi commander of the bodyguard, the lala royal tutor, the regional beglerbegs) through the early Safavid century, and the great civil war of 1576-1590 between the Ustajlu and Shamlu factions nearly breaks the dynasty. Shah Abbas I builds the ghulam corps precisely to escape this dependence; the institution remains a powerful military reservoir, but at the price of perpetually empowering the uymaq chiefs.

list.name: Tofangchi Musket Corps
list.text: The standing musketeer infantry instituted by Shah Abbas I as part of his post-1590 military reform, drawn largely from the Persian-speaking peasantry of the central plateau rather than from the Turcoman tribes. Trained by Robert Sherley and the English advisors who reach Qazvin in 1598, the tofangchi are the throne's answer to the Janissary musket-line that bloodied the Safavids at Chaldiran in 1514, and they pair with the new tupchi (artillery) corps to give Persia a powder-and-shot army independent of the cavalry confederacy. The tofangchi number perhaps twelve thousand at Abbas's death; recruitment from the villages is the price the peasantry pays.

list.name: Mostowfi-ul-Mamalik
list.text: Chief Accountant of the Realm, head of the Diwan-i-Mostowfi, who maintains the registers of every iqta and tuyul assignment, audits the provincial mostowfis under him, and presents the annual budget (dastur al-amal) to the shah and the Grand Vizier. The office traces through Buyid and Seljuq practice into the Safavid state, where Mirza Salman Jaberi's reorganization of the 1570s standardizes the registers; under the Qajar shahs, Mirza Aqa Khan Nuri and Amir Kabir each use the office to attempt fiscal reform against the appanages of the princes. A working mostowfiya prevents officers from drawing salaries from villages already assigned to another, the chief pathology of every Iranian fiscal regime.

list.name: Mamalik-i-Mahrusa
list.text: The 'Guarded Domains' appanage system of the Qajar dynasty, by which the shah's adult sons and brothers are appointed governors-general of the great provinces (Abbas Mirza in Tabriz over Azerbaijan, Mohammad Ali Mirza in Kermanshah, Hosayn Ali Mirza Farmanfarma in Shiraz over Fars) each holding court, levying taxes, raising regiments, and signing treaties with foreign envoys as a sub-monarch under the throne of Tehran. The system extends Qajar reach across a realm without a working postal service or paid bureaucracy, but the princely courts run their own armies, contract their own loans with Russian and British agents, and frequently fight one another upon a shah's death. The succession of 1834, which required British intervention to seat Mohammad Shah, was the system's natural product.
